planting.note: Set out container stock after the last frost so roots establish before summer heat; fall planting also works in milder parts of its range.

directions: This evergreen South Texas shrub carries aromatic, citrus-scented compound leaves and clusters of small cream flowers nearly year-round, drawing butterflies and other pollinators. It tolerates the caliche and sandy loam soils typical of Rio Grande Plains thornscrub and needs only occasional watering once its roots are established. Site it in a partially shaded understory spot beneath taller thorn-forest trees for the best foliage color, though it will take more sun with a bit more moisture. Light pruning after bloom flushes keeps the form tidy without reducing flowering.
sources: USDA Forest Service Fire Effects Information System

planting.note: Divide rhizome clumps or set out rooted offsets in spring once soil has warmed; avoid wet, poorly drained sites.

directions: A low, colony-forming succulent of Tamaulipan thornscrub, leatherstem spreads by underground rhizomes into loose thickets of slender, leathery stems that bleed a clear sap turning blood-red on contact with air. It thrives in rocky or caliche soils with sharp drainage and needs essentially no supplemental water once established, making it a fitting edging or rock-garden plant for Gulf Coast xeriscapes. Keep it away from standing water or heavy clay, which quickly rots the rhizomes. Handle with care, as the sap and foliage are irritating to skin and toxic if ingested by people or livestock.

planting.note: Scarify or hot-water-soak seed before sowing; set container plants after the last frost into well-drained, alkaline soil.

directions: Blackbrush acacia forms a dense, thorny thicket of fine, dark foliage across Rio Grande Plains limestone and caliche rises, bursting into fragrant cream-yellow puffball flowers in late winter that are prized by beekeepers for an early honey flow. It handles rocky, alkaline, low-fertility ground with ease and asks for no irrigation beyond its establishment year. Give it full sun and room to spread, since the stiff thorny branches make a very effective barrier hedge or wildlife thicket. Prune only to shape, as this species resents heavy cutting back.
sources: USDA Forest Service Fire Effects Information System

planting.note: Transplant container stock in spring; seed benefits from scarification before sowing.

directions: This tough deciduous shrub of South Texas brushland shows off distinctive zig-zagging gray branches and mottled bark even in winter, with small greenish flowers followed by dark fruit that birds favor. It is well adapted to the thin, rocky or caliche soils of thornscrub and takes dry conditions in stride once rooted. Use it in a wildlife hedgerow or mixed-brush screen where its angular winter silhouette adds structure. Minimal pruning is needed beyond removing dead wood.

planting.note: Install container-grown plants in spring into well-drained, rocky or caliche soil; drought once established.

directions: Known locally as oreja de raton, this dense evergreen shrub of South Texas limestone brush country carries small scalloped leaves and inconspicuous flowers on separate male and female plants, followed by woolly seed capsules on females. It is unfussy about soil fertility but insists on sharp drainage, thriving on the rocky hillsides and caliche outcrops typical of Tamaulipan thornscrub. Use it as dense infill in a native hedgerow or wildlife thicket, where it provides cover and browse. It needs little attention beyond occasional shaping.

planting.note: Set out container stock in spring after frost danger passes; tolerates coastal salt spray and alkaline soils.

directions: Saffron plum is a spiny evergreen shrub or small tree of South Texas and Gulf Coast thornscrub and coastal brush, producing small greenish-white flowers over much of the year and sweet blue-black drupes that are heavily browsed by deer and birds. Its dense, glossy foliage and tolerance for salt, wind, and alkaline or sandy soils suit it well to coastal hedgerows and wildlife plantings. Give it full sun and let it go dry between waterings once established, as it is adapted to the sparse rainfall of the Rio Grande Plains. The stout thorns make it a useful living barrier as well as a wildlife food source.

planting.note: Scarify seed before sowing, or set out container-grown saplings in spring after the last frost.

directions: Twisted acacia is a small, thorny multi-trunked tree of the Rio Grande Plains, named for its gnarled, contorted branching, and it lights up in early spring with fragrant golden puffball flowers that feed a wide range of pollinators. It is well suited to caliche, limestone, or sandy thornscrub soils and needs little water beyond its first season or two in the ground. Use it as a specimen or in a native thorn-forest grove where its open, picturesque form and dappled shade can be appreciated. Fuzzy seed pods that follow the flowers are readily eaten by browsing wildlife and livestock.
sources: USDA Forest Service Fire Effects Information System
